FrMS88-de2619-d1e111.summary: Announces, after treating the univocation of being, four questions on its mode, and poses the first: whether being is said quidditatively of the divine essence in its ultimate precision. The negative argument cites Anselm's De veritate: as the shining is to light, so essence to being; but light is said only denominatively of the shining.
claims: Anselm's analogy suggests being is said only denominatively of the divine essence.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e129.summary: Contrary: Augustine (De Trinitate V) says that 'essence' is said most properly of God.
claims: 'Essence' is said most properly of God.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e134.summary: Sets out four conclusions of 'the Doctor' (Scotus): being is not said quidditatively of anything simply simple, nor of the primarily diverse, nor of the proper attributes of being, nor of ultimate differences.
claims: Being is not said quidditatively of the simply simple, the primarily diverse, its attributes, or ultimate differences.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e145.summary: Defines a simply simple concept as one not resolvable into other concepts, like the indivisible point in quantity, and proves that such concepts exist: otherwise there would be an infinite regress among essentially ordered quidditative concepts.
claims: A simply simple concept is one not resolvable into other concepts.
Simply simple concepts exist, on pain of infinite regress.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e162.summary: Proves the first conclusion: when something common is quidditatively included in an inferior, the inferior is resolvable into a common and a proper notion; nothing simply simple is resolvable.
claims: Being is not quidditatively included in the simply simple.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e180.summary: Second conclusion: nothing is predicated in quid of the primarily diverse. Explains the term: when things agree and differ, one must reach included items that differ so as to agree in nothing, else an infinite regress; these ultimates are the primarily diverse.
claims: Primarily diverse items agree in nothing.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e191.summary: Argues the second conclusion: whatever includes the notion of being agrees in something, but the primarily diverse agree in nothing.
claims: Being is not included in the primarily diverse.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e198.summary: Proves the third conclusion, about attributes: no proper attribute is more perfect than its subject, but if being were included in its attributes, an attribute would be more perfect than being by adding its proper notion, since what includes another and more is more perfect.
claims: Being is not included quidditatively in its proper attributes.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e209.summary: Proves the fourth conclusion: ultimate differences are primarily diverse, and nothing is common to the primarily diverse.
claims: Being is not included in ultimate differences.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e216.summary: Shows also that being is not included in the first differences: what is divided immediately into certain items is not included quidditatively in them, else there would be redundancy (adding the divided to the dividing), and being is divided immediately by its first differences. Then raises four objections, the first being that everything known is resolved into the notion of being, and the simply simple can be known.
claims: Being is not included quidditatively in its first dividing differences.
Objection: whatever is known is resolved into being.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e233.summary: Second objection: the primarily diverse is either quidditatively being or quidditatively nothing; it is not nothing, so it is being.
claims: Objection: the primarily diverse must be quidditatively being.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e238.summary: Third objection: no predication in the abstract is true unless quidditative, but in the abstract 'truth' receives the predication of being.
claims: Objection: abstract predications of being must be quidditative.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e245.summary: Fourth objection: ultimate differences are specific differences, and these include being, since 'rational' is a being.
claims: Objection: specific differences like 'rational' include being.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e252.summary: Reply to the first objection: there are two kinds of resolution — into essential parts, in the categorial line, where the resolvents are said in quid; and into priors that are not essential parts, which need not be said in quid of what is resolved into them.
claims: Resolution into non-essential priors does not entail quidditative predication.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e265.summary: Reply to the second objection: the primarily diverse are being, though not quidditatively, yet not quidditatively nothing; contradictories with an added determination lose the nature of contradiction, as a man is neither per se white nor per se non-white.
claims: The primarily diverse are being, but not quidditatively.
Contradictories qualified by a determination such as 'quidditatively' may both be false.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e278.summary: Reply to the third objection: not only quidditative but also identical predication is true in abstracts, as in divine matters; but in God identical predication is granted because of infinity, whereas here because of the commonness of the other, exceeding extreme, being.
claims: Identical (non-quidditative) predication can be true in the abstract.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e290.summary: Reply to the fourth objection: first differences are those by which being is first divided (absolute and respective) and do not include being quidditatively; ultimate differences are individual properties or specific differences taken from the ultimate reality, where the resolution of quidditative concepts ends; 'rational' is not taken from ultimate reality but is further resolved. Then introduces four conclusions of Thomas Anglicus, compatible with the preceding: being is not included quidditatively in any category, subalternate genus, lowest species, or individual of any category.
claims: First differences of being (absolute and respective) do not include being quidditatively.
Ultimate differences are those taken from the ultimate reality where resolution ends.
Being is not quidditatively included in categories, subalternate genera, lowest species, or individuals.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e323.summary: Proves the first of Thomas' conclusions: the categories are the first irresolvables; if being were quidditatively included in them they would be resolvable.
claims: Categories are first irresolvables and do not include being quidditatively.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e332.summary: Second conclusion: when two formal notions are quidditatively included in something they must be subordinated; a subalternate genus includes its categorial genus, which neither includes nor is included in being.
claims: Being is not quidditatively included in subalternate genera.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e343.summary: Third conclusion: the definition of a lowest species consists of genus and difference, but being is neither genus nor difference nor included in them.
claims: Being is not quidditatively included in lowest species.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e350.summary: Fourth conclusion: the whole quiddity of individuals is the species, in which being is not included. Then raises four difficulties, the first about priority: what is not said in quid of things is not prior to them, so being would not be prior to them, which is manifestly false.
claims: Being is not quidditatively included in individuals.
Objection: being would not be prior if not said in quid.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e372.summary: Second difficulty: every predicate is per se or per accidens; being is not per accidens, so per se, either in the first mode (hence in quid) or the second mode, which is posterior and accidental-like, which is false of being.
claims: Objection: per se predication of being must be first mode and thus in quid.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e384.summary: Third difficulty: predication of a genus of a difference seems accidental; if the predication of being is reduced to it, it will be accidental.
claims: Objection: genus-of-difference predication seems accidental.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e391.summary: Fourth difficulty: being is certainly predicated univocally, but what is predicated denominatively is not predicated univocally.
claims: Objection: denominative predication cannot be univocal.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e398.summary: Reply to the first difficulty: denies that what is not predicated quidditatively cannot be prior — a genus is not predicated quidditatively of its difference yet is prior; what is predicated in quid is prior, but not conversely.
claims: Priority does not require quidditative predication.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e409.summary: Reply to the second: being is predicated not as in the second mode but in the first, though not directly — only indirectly and by reduction.
claims: Being is predicated in the first mode of per se predication indirectly, by reduction.
concepts: first mode of per se predication

FrMS88-de2619-d1e416.summary: Reply to the third: a genus is predicated of a difference per se, not per accidens, since there is an essential order between them, prior even to the order of genus to species (which is through the difference); this predication reduces to the first mode, like predication of one essential part of another.
claims: Genus is predicated per se of difference, by an essential order reducible to the first mode.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e434.summary: Reply to the fourth: denominative predication is twofold — from something posterior and accidental (never univocal, as 'just' from justice) or from something essentially prior (which can be univocal, being reducible to the first mode, like genus of difference and the predication of transcendentals). Determines the question: being is said of the divine essence neither as essential part nor as genus of species, but as genus of difference.
claims: Denominative predication from an essential prior can be univocal.
Being is said of the divine essence as a genus is of a difference, not as an essential part or as genus of species.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e459.summary: First proof: whatever is included in a quiddity as an essential part is prior to it; nothing is prior to the deity, so nothing is included in its quiddity in the first mode as an essential part.
claims: Nothing is prior to the deity, so nothing is an essential part of it.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e468.summary: Second proof: the divine essence is a simply simple perfection, and such a perfection includes nothing as its part.
claims: The divine essence is a simply simple perfection without parts.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e477.summary: Third proof: nothing common is quidditatively included in the primarily diverse, and the divine essence is primarily diverse, as will be shown later.
claims: The divine essence is primarily diverse.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e484.summary: Fourth proof: according to Dionysius, the divine essence is the root of all divine perfections, and nothing can be the root of what belongs to its own quiddity. Then raises four difficulties, the first asking why being is not predicated quidditatively of the divine essence as other superiors are.
claims: The divine essence is the root of all divine perfections.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e497.summary: Answers that it has been shown being is said of the divine essence denominatively, not quidditatively; if it were included quidditatively in something else, that would be more intimately a being than God. Objection: the notion of being is said quidditatively of this individual being, which then would be more intimately a being than God.
claims: Being is said denominatively of the divine essence.
Objection: an individual being would be more intimately being than God.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e513.summary: Further objection: animal is said quidditatively of man, so man would be an animal more intimately than God is a being.
claims: Objection: quidditative predication would make creatures more intimately what they are than God is being.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e519.summary: Reply: denies that this individual would be more a being than God, since more and less are measured by quantity of power, and the notion of God is per se prior to the notion of being.
claims: Degrees of being are measured by power, and God's notion is prior to that of being.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e528.summary: To the rejoinder that this individual is at least more intimately a being than God, replies that one need not posit so total an identity between God and being as between a thing and itself.
claims: God and being are not identical in the way a thing is identical with itself.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e537.summary: Reply to the other objection: it is granted that, in a way more evident to us, man is an animal more than God is a being (in the first mode of per se predication), yet the mode of identity in God is simply more powerful and perfect.
claims: The identity of God with being is simply more perfect, though less evident to us than quidditative predication.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e546.summary: Second difficulty: although a superior divided by differences is not of their quiddity, it seems to be of the quiddity of what they constitute; why then is being, divided by absolute and respective, not of the quiddity of what they constitute?
claims: Objection: being seems to be of the quiddity of what its differences constitute.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e562.summary: Reply: division of transcendentals differs from division of genera; because genus and difference are limited they compose one thing, but because transcendentals and their differences are unlimited they constitute no third thing, being simply simple since found in God.
claims: Transcendentals and their differences, being unlimited, do not compose a third thing.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e575.summary: Third difficulty, about intrinsic modes: the predication of being of finite being seems quidditative, since an intrinsic mode does not vary the quidditative notion.
claims: Objection: being is predicated quidditatively of finite being.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e585.summary: Reply: the predication of being of finite being is quidditative, not in the sense that being and the mode compose one formal notion receiving the predicate, but in that the being which is finite is being; being is said not of finitude but of what is determined by finitude, as 'animal' is said of a white man rather than as of the notion composed of animal and rational.
claims: Being is predicated quidditatively of finite being as of what is determined by finitude, not of the mode itself.
Being and its intrinsic mode do not compose a single formal notion.

FrMS88-de2619-d1e607.summary: Fourth difficulty: whether the first mode of per se predication is found in God. Answer: not properly, since there is nothing definable or defining there; but there is such a mode by reduction, not as an essential part but as genus of difference.
claims: In God the first mode of per se predication is found only by reduction.
concepts: first mode of per se predication

FrMS88-de2619-d1e620.summary: Reply to the opening argument: 'shining' is a participle and so said denominatively; likewise 'being' as a participle, but not as a noun taken from essence or quiddity.
claims: 'Being' taken as a participle is said denominatively, but not as a noun signifying essence.

FrMS88-de2619.summary: Opening a group of four questions on the mode of the univocation of being, the sixth question of the prologue asks whether being is said quidditatively of the divine essence taken in its ultimate precision. Meyronnes first presents four conclusions of 'the Doctor' (Scotus): being is not said quidditatively of the simply simple, the primarily diverse, the proper attributes of being, or the ultimate differences, since what includes a common notion is resolvable, the primarily diverse agree in nothing, an attribute including being would be more perfect than its subject, and being is divided immediately by its first differences. He answers objections by distinguishing resolution into essential parts from resolution into non-essential priors, and by restricting 'ultimate differences' to those taken from ultimate reality. He then adds four compatible conclusions of Thomas Anglicus (being is not quidditatively in categories, subalternate genera, lowest species, or individuals) and defends against difficulties the view that the predication of being is per se, reducible to the first mode indirectly, like that of a genus of a difference, and so can be denominative yet univocal. His own determination: being is said of the divine essence neither as an essential part nor as genus of species, but as genus of difference, because nothing is prior to deity, the divine essence is a simply simple perfection, it is primarily diverse, and (per Dionysius) it is the root of all divine perfections. Further difficulties are resolved: an individual being is not thereby 'more intimately being' than God; transcendentals divided by their differences constitute no third thing; being is predicated of finite being as of what is determined by the intrinsic mode, not of the mode; and in God the first mode of per se predication exists only by reduction.
claims: Being is not said quidditatively of the simply simple, the primarily diverse, the proper attributes of being, or ultimate differences.
Being is not included quidditatively in categories, subalternate genera, lowest species, or individuals.
The predication of being is per se and reducible to the first mode, like the predication of a genus of a difference; it can be denominative and still univocal.
Being is said of the divine essence neither as an essential part nor as a genus of a species, but as a genus of a difference.
Transcendentals and their differences, being unlimited, do not compose a third thing.
Being is predicated of finite being as of the being determined by finitude, not of the intrinsic mode itself.
concepts: first mode of per se predication
divine essence as root of perfections
